business: Battery-backed washing machine (working name): a semi-automatic washer with a built-in battery that finishes a load during a power cut, charged from the grid when power is on or from an optional solar panel
by_segment: Hamlet with weak or no grid, uses a solar home system
why_not: Twenty-two thousand is two months of what the whole family earns, and ₹2,000 every month for a year is more than we can promise when the harvest money is uncertain. The women already wash by hand and it costs us nothing, so this is not where our money goes first.

₹22,000 is most of a month's family income and every rupee right now is going to the wedding fund. Even ₹2,000 a month for a year is a new bill I can't take on just so a washer finishes when the light goes; we can wait for the power or wash by hand.

Our water only comes for a short time each day, so the power cut is not the real problem. A battery does nothing when the tank is empty. And with the wedding money being saved, ₹22,000, or ₹2,000 every month for a year, on a washing machine is not happening.

We already have an inverter in the house, and if it struggles with a washer I can buy a bigger battery for it, which also keeps the fans and lights running. Paying twenty-two thousand for a washer with its own battery that only does two cold loads feels like paying twice for the same thing, and nobody I know has one yet.

Twenty-two thousand is about a month and more of what our whole house earns, and nobody I know has used a washing machine that runs on a battery. I won't put that money down until someone in the family or the neighbour has had one working for a season.

The power cuts are a real trouble for me, but I only buy brands I see on TV like LG or Samsung, and here nobody tells me whose machine this is. ₹21,999 is nearly double a normal semi-automatic, and I will not put that much into a name I don't know just because the local dealer says so.

We have always washed by hand at home and it costs nothing, so I don't feel any need for a machine at all, let alone one with a battery. I can afford ₹22,000, but I would rather put that money into the farm or the shop.

We have always washed by hand at the tap and it works fine for us. Without steady power the borewell often isn't running anyway, so a machine that finishes its load on battery doesn't fix my real water problem.

Every rupee we can spare is going into the wedding fund right now, and the women at home already wash by hand for free. Adding a ₹2,000 EMI every month for a year just so the washing finishes during a power cut is not something I can justify this year.

I am not buying a big machine in an ordinary week at full price. Hand-washing costs us nothing, and if I buy a washer at all it will be at the harvest or for a wedding in the family, when the dealer gives a discount or a free gift.
